hist-anc-01-c2.text: National Geographic. How the Rosetta Stone unlocked the secrets of ancient civilizations. National Geographic.
hist-anc-01-c2.quote: When Pierre-François Bouchard's men discovered the ancient stone slab that would change the world on July 19, 1799, they weren't on an archaeological dig; they were doing a last-minute construction job.
hist-anc-01-c2.claim: The Rosetta Stone, discovered in 1799, finally let scholars read hieroglyphs.

hist-anc-02-c3.text: Joshua J. Mark (2018). Augustus. World History Encyclopedia.
hist-anc-02-c3.quote: Augustus Caesar (27 BCE - 14 CE) was the name of the first and, by most accounts, greatest Roman emperor.
hist-anc-02-c3.claim: Civil wars produced strongmen: Julius Caesar, then his adopted heir Augustus, who became Rome's first emperor in 27 BCE.

hist-anc-03-c2.text: Mark Cartwright (2013). Battle of Thermopylae. World History Encyclopedia.
hist-anc-03-c2.quote: In 490 BCE Greek forces led by Athens met the Persians in battle at Marathon and defeated the invaders.
hist-anc-03-c2.claim: At Marathon (490 BCE), Athens defeated a Persian invasion force.

hist-anc-04-c2.text: Joshua J. Mark (2012). Shi Huangdi. World History Encyclopedia.
hist-anc-04-c2.quote: Shi Huangdi (l.259-210 BCE/r.221-210 BCE, also known as Qin Shi Huang, Qin Shih Huandi, Shi Huangti or Shih Huan-ti) was the first emperor of a unified China.
hist-anc-04-c2.claim: China's first unified empire came under Qin Shi Huang in 221 BCE.

hist-anc-04-c2.text: Joshua J. Mark (2020). Han Dynasty. World History Encyclopedia.
hist-anc-04-c2.quote: The Han Dynasty (202 BCE - 220 CE) was the second dynasty of Imperial China (the era of centralized, dynastic government, 221 BCE - 1912 CE) which established the paradigm for all succeeding dynasties up through 1912 CE.
hist-anc-04-c2.claim: The succeeding Han Dynasty (202 BCE – 220 CE) ran for over 400 years and is what gave China much of its enduring identity.

hist-anc-05-c2.text: Donald L. Wasson (2013). Constantine I. World History Encyclopedia.
hist-anc-05-c2.quote: Realizing that the Roman Empire was too large for one man to adequately rule, Emperor Diocletian (284-305 CE) split the empire into two, creating a tetrachy or rule of four.
hist-anc-05-c2.claim: Diocletian (r. 284–305 CE) reformed the empire to make it manageable.

hist-anc-05-c2.text: Donald L. Wasson (2013). Constantine I. World History Encyclopedia.
hist-anc-05-c2.quote: While he ruled the east from Nicomedia as an “augustus” with Galerius as his “caesar,” Maximian and Constantius the Pale ruled the west.
hist-anc-05-c2.claim: He split administration in two, a Western emperor and an Eastern emperor, each with a junior co-emperor (the Tetrarchy).

hist-anc-06-c2.text: Joshua J. Mark (2011). Writing: The Preservation of Human Thought and Action. World History Encyclopedia.
hist-anc-06-c2.quote: The first writer in history known by name is the Akkadian high priestess Enheduanna (circa 2300 BCE)
hist-anc-06-c2.claim: The first known author named in records is Enheduanna, an Akkadian priestess (~2300 BCE).
